passage:
Note from the reception class, Pooja. Sarita opened a hospital in the book corner today. She made stethoscopes from wool and handed out roles: "You are the nurse, you are the patient." When Imran laughed during an injection she stopped everything. "Doctors don't laugh, it scares the patient." The children reset without adult help.
Later she spoke softly to a soft-toy patient: "It won't hurt much. I'm here." I stayed nearby and did not direct. Tomorrow I will bring some old bandage rolls for the corner.

qa.q: What did Sarita make the stethoscopes from?
qa.a: She made them from wool.

qa.q: What does Sarita seem to feel about the hospital game being spoiled?
qa.a: She takes the game seriously and wants it to feel real. She is protective of the pretend patient, so she stops the game when someone laughs.

qa.q: What did Pooja choose to do while the hospital game went on?
qa.a: Pooja stayed nearby without directing, then planned to bring some old bandage rolls to extend the play.

qa.q: How might Imran feel when Sarita stops the game?
qa.a: Imran may feel a little told off or embarrassed, but the children reset the game themselves, so the story carries on.

grounding: A child runs a make-believe hospital, assigning roles and correcting others who break the story.

Under the neem tree behind the house, Ira had opened her shop. Pebbles were rice, leaves were notes, and a cracked plate was the scale.
"You must pay first," she told her aunt Rekha, who held out a crumpled leaf. "That one is torn. Not allowed."
Rekha smiled, fetched a fresh leaf, and Ira weighed out three pebbles with great care. "Come again," she said, exactly the way the shopkeeper in the village does, and pushed her braid back.
Then she frowned at the goat, which had wandered into the queue, and shooed it to the back.

qa.q: What did the pebbles stand for in Ira's shop?
qa.a: The pebbles were rice.

qa.q: What does Ira seem to feel about her shop rules?
qa.a: She feels important and in charge. She takes the rules seriously, refusing a torn leaf and copying the shopkeeper's 'Come again'.

qa.q: What choice by Rekha keeps Ira's game going?
qa.a: Rekha follows the rules and plays along, fetching a fresh leaf instead of arguing, so Ira stays in charge.

qa.q: What might Rekha be enjoying while she plays customer?
qa.a: Rekha may enjoy seeing how carefully Ira copies grown-up life, as her smile suggests.

grounding: A child runs a make-believe shop and corrects those who break its rules.

Under the neem tree behind their house in the village, Sachin set up a shop on a jute sack: pebbles for potatoes, neem leaves for money, an old tin for the till. "Pooja, you're the customer. Ravi, you're the delivery man."
Pooja picked up a pebble and pretended to eat it. "No!" Sachin said. "You have to pay first. That's the rule of shops."
Pooja handed over three leaves. Sachin counted them seriously, put them in the tin, and wrapped the pebble in a leaf. "Come again tomorrow."

qa.q: What did Sachin use as money?
qa.a: Neem leaves.

qa.q: Why did Sachin say "No!" when Pooja pretended to eat the pebble?
qa.a: He was annoyed that it broke the shop's rule; he wanted the game to work like a real shop, where you pay first.

qa.q: What is Sachin practising in this game?
qa.a: How a shop works: giving roles, taking payment, counting, and politely saying "Come again tomorrow".

qa.q: What might the game be like for Pooja?
qa.a: Pooja gets to play along and learn the shop rules from Sachin, even when corrected.

grounding: Shows a child running a pretend shop, assigning roles and correcting a player who breaks the story.

passage:
In their small apartment in Marseille, Leila turned the sofa into a hospital. The cushions were beds. Her little sister Fatima was the patient, and teddy was the other patient.
"You have a broken leg," Leila announced, wrapping a scarf around Fatima's ankle. "Say ouch."
"Ouch."
Fatima tried to get up. "No, no, you can't walk, you're in hospital! Nurses bring the food." Leila fetched a plate of grapes and fed her one. Then she took teddy's temperature with a pencil and frowned very seriously. "He needs to sleep."

qa.q: What did Leila wrap around Fatima's ankle?
qa.a: A scarf.

qa.q: Why did Leila stop Fatima from getting up?
qa.a: Leila was worried the hospital story would break, since patients with broken legs can't walk, and she took her job as the one in charge seriously.

qa.q: What is Leila learning through this game?
qa.a: How caring for someone works: rules for patients, bringing food and checking temperature, all in a safe pretend frame.

qa.q: What might Fatima enjoy about being the patient?
qa.a: Fatima gets fussed over, fed grapes and looked after by her big sister.

grounding: Shows a child running a pretend hospital, assigning roles and keeping others to the story's rules.

In the kindergarten play corner, Manjula lined up six small chairs in two rows. "This is the bus to Mysore. Sahil, you're the driver. I'm the conductor."
She tore scraps of paper into tickets. "Ticket, ticket!" Each child got one.
Sahil drove for a bit, then turned round and started eating his snack. "Driver can't eat!" Manjula said, hands on hips. "We'll crash!" Sahil put the biscuit away and gripped the plate that was the steering wheel.
The teacher watched from her desk, smiling, as Manjula rang the pretend bell. "Next stop, Nani's house!"

qa.q: What did Manjula tear the paper into?
qa.a: Tickets.

qa.q: Why did Manjula put her hands on her hips at Sahil?
qa.a: She was annoyed that he broke the bus rules, and worried, inside the story, that they'd crash.

qa.q: How could the teacher support this play?
qa.a: The teacher could let it run, perhaps offering a real bell or ticket paper, without taking over Manjula's story.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel being corrected?
qa.a: Sahil might feel a bit told off but goes along, putting the biscuit away and gripping the wheel.

grounding: Shows a child running a pretend bus, giving roles and correcting a player who steps out of the story.

passage:
Monday. Rajni set up a hospital under the dining table with a dupatta for a curtain. "I'm Doctor. Gargi, you're the patient. You have fever."
Gargi giggled and said, "No, I'm a lion!"
"Lions can't come to hospital!" Rajni said, very seriously. "Lie down, patient."
Wednesday. Rajni gave Gargi a toy stethoscope. "Now you're the nurse. Nurses are kind. Say, 'Don't cry, it won't hurt.'"
Gargi said it to the teddy.
Saturday. Rajni's teddy fell off the bed. She held it close and whispered, "Don't cry. Doctor is here. It won't hurt." Then she bandaged it very carefully.

qa.q: What did Rajni use for a curtain?
qa.a: Rajni used a dupatta for a curtain.

qa.q: Why did Rajni say "Lions can't come to hospital!" so seriously?
qa.a: Rajni felt strongly that the story had rules, and was a little annoyed that Gargi was breaking them.

qa.q: What was Rajni practising in this pretend hospital?
qa.a: She was rehearsing how grown-ups care for someone who is hurt, like comforting and bandaging, in a safe, make-believe way.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel about being told what role to play?
qa.a: Gargi seems happy and amused, giggling and going along, though Gargi might wish to be a lion sometimes.

grounding: A child runs a make-believe hospital, assigning roles and correcting others, rehearsing care and rules in a safe frame.
